title: The Free Kick That Turned Into a Spiral

lines: This free kick was flying wide. Then it turned.
Roberto Carlos hit it with the outside of his left foot, from far out.
The ball swung around the wall and kept heading wide.
Then it bent back in, past a goalkeeper who never moved.
Spin pushes the ball sideways. Drag slows the ball down, but the spin keeps going.
So the slower it flies, the tighter it curves, into a spiral.
That is why the bend came so late. Every goal has a story.

traceability.purpose: Hook: low floodlit camera behind the ball and the wall; the ball flies out wide of the post, then visibly turns back. The question is asked by the picture before the words finish.

evidence.claim: The ball swerved around the French wall and appeared to be heading wide before bending back into the goal.
evidence.source: Sky Sports; What A Howler; ESPN

evidence.claim: Model used for the animated trajectories: point ball with quadratic drag (Cd 0.25) and Magnus lift from the spin ratio, integrated with RK4; launch values are chosen for the illustration, not measured from the 1997 kick.

traceability.purpose: Place and date as a stadium scoreboard: an original dot-matrix board lights up LYON, 3 JUNE 1997, then the fixture, over the floodlit stands.

evidence.claim: Roberto Carlos scored a free kick for Brazil against France on 3 June 1997 at the Stade de Gerland in Lyon, in the opening match of the Tournoi de France, which ended 1-1.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, 1997 Tournoi de France; Sky Sports (skysports.com/football/news/11095/10899358)

traceability.purpose: The strike in close-up: a boot swings in and meets the ball off-centre with its outside edge; the contact sets the ball spinning (arrow). Shape of the contact, not a likeness.

evidence.claim: He struck the ball with the outside of his left foot from long range; reported distances vary from about 33 metres to 40 yards.
evidence.source: What A Howler; Sky Sports; Chalkdust Magazine

traceability.purpose: Thirteen years later: the timeline runs from 1997 to 2010 and a journal page slides in with the paper's title and authors, the source of the explanation that follows.

evidence.claim: In 2010 Guillaume Dupeux, Anne Le Goff, David Quere and Christophe Clanet published 'The spinning ball spiral' in New Journal of Physics 12, 093004.

traceability.purpose: The mechanism in the ball's frame: spin speeds the air on one side and the sideways force appears; then drag appears and the air (ball) slows while the spin gauge holds; the flow pattern grows more lopsided.

evidence.claim: The paper shows that a spinning ball slowed by drag, while its spin stays nearly constant, follows a path that curves more and more tightly, a spiral; the authors use Roberto Carlos's 1997 free kick as the example of a ball that began to follow this spiral.
evidence.source: ScienceDaily; Physics World; APS DFD 2009 abstract 'The Roberto Carlos Spiral'
